newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan cautious on further China shipping links.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan cautious on further China shipping links.

text.p: A Taiwan cabinet agency on Tuesday said it was considering wider shipping exchanges with rival China and possibly even direct cargo swaps, but that progress depended on the political atmosphere.

The Mainland Affairs Council, which makes policy toward communist China, said it was considering allowing western Taichung and northern Keelung ports to join a quasi-direct shipping scheme pioneered in April at southern Kaohsiung.

Council official Chang Shu-li said proposals to relax restrictions on what goods could actually enter Taiwan customs also were under consideration, but he cautioned that progress hinged on the extent of Taiwan-China cooperation.
"It is our plan to introduce more ports to link with the mainland and to ease restrictions on cargoes to enter our customs, but we don't have a timetable for that," Chang told Reuters by telephone.
"Taichung and Keelung are being considered, but when they will start links with the mainland depends on the atmosphere between the sides," Chang added.
The rivals have not been on talking terms since mid-1995.

Nevertheless in April, Taipei eased a ban dating back to 1949 and allowed selected mainland and Taiwanese companies to begin sailing direct routes between its southern port of Kaohsiung and two nearby mainland ports, Xiamen and Fuzhou.
Despite the breakthrough, the service remains restricted.

Incoming mainland cargoes cannot enter Taiwanese customs and must be transshipped onward to third destinations. Likewise, Taiwanese cargoes cannot be put aboard ships that will be crossing directly to the mainland.

Taipei's China Times said on Tuesday that the council had proposed adding Keelung and Taichung to the scheme, and quoted unidentified sources as saying Beijing in return may consider allowing more mainland ports to start direct Taiwan routes.
More significantly, the paper quoted sources as saying the council was considering allowing limited direct exchanges of Chinese and Taiwanese cargoes for the first time in 48 years.
Council official Chang declined to comment in detail, but said Taipei did not rule out allowing direct cargo exchanges.

Tens of thousands of Taiwanese firms that have invested more than US$30 billion on the mainland have pressured Taipei to allow direct cargo exchanges, saying transshipping them via Hong Kong as is now required adds unnecessary cost and delays.
Taipei banned Taiwan Strait crossings in 1949 after China's civil war left the communists in control of the mainland and the defeated nationalists in exile on Taiwan.
Taipei remains reluctant to allow direct cargo exchanges, wary of weakening its political position against the communist government in Beijing.
Beijing regards Taiwan as a renegade province that must eventually be brought under mainland rule.

Taipei accepts the idea of eventual reunification, but only after the Communist Party drops its monopoly on power and allows multiparty democracy. In the meantime, Taiwan allows unofficial economic and personal links with China but no official ties.

Beijing in mid-1995 broke off what had been slowly warming semi-official talks after Taiwan's President Lee Teng-hui made a private U.S. visit. Beijing assailed the trip as a push toward Taiwan's independence and away from reunification with China.
